Tabernacle
TAB-er-nak-ul
noun (biblical theology / Old Testament worship / typology)
Latin tabernaculum (tent, hut, temporary dwelling), diminutive of taberna (shed, tavern); used in the Vulgate to translate Hebrew mishkan (“dwelling place, sanctuary”) and 'ohel mo'ed (“tent of meeting”); the mishkan is from the root shakan (to dwell, to tabernacle) — the same root as the later post-biblical concept of the Shekinah (the visible glory of the divine presence); God commanded the construction of the tabernacle in Exodus 25–31 and 35–40 as a portable sanctuary for the wilderness years and the early period of settlement in Canaan

See also: Tabernacle

Biblical Definition

The tabernacle is the portable wilderness sanctuary that YHWH commanded Moses to build according to the precise pattern shown him on Mount Sinai (Exod 25:9, 40), so that God might dwell in the midst of His people (Exod 25:8: “Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them”). Its structure embodied graduated approach to God: the outer court (accessible to all Israel) with the bronze altar of burnt offering and the bronze laver; the Holy Place (accessible only to priests) containing the lampstand, the table of showbread, and the altar of incense; and the Most Holy Place (accessible only to the high priest once a year on Yom Kippur) containing the ark of the covenant beneath the cherubim. The spatial gradient — from outer court to Holy Place to Most Holy Place — symbolized the graduated holiness of God's presence and the barrier of sin that prevented direct human approach. Every element was typologically loaded: the ark and its mercy seat prefigured Christ as the propitiation (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2); the lampstand prefigured Christ as the light of the world (John 8:12); the showbread prefigured Christ as the bread of life (John 6:35); the bronze altar prefigured Christ as the burnt offering bearing divine wrath; the veil that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place was torn at Christ's death (Matt 27:51). Hebrews 8–10 is the systematic typological exposition: the tabernacle and its priesthood were “Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount.” (Heb 8:5); Christ entered the true tabernacle “not made with hands” (Heb 9:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

TABERNACLE: the portable wilderness sanctuary of Israel, commanded by God in Exodus 25–40 as a dwelling-place among His people; its tripartite structure (outer court, Holy Place, Most Holy Place) typologically anticipated Christ's atoning work as described in Hebrews 8–10; John 1:14 (“the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us”) applies the tabernacle imagery to the Incarnation.

TABERNACLE. n. [L. tabernaculum, a small tent.] The portable sanctuary constructed by Israel in the wilderness under God's specific instruction to Moses (Exod 25–31; 35–40); a framed tent structure covered with progressively more valuable materials from outside (goats' hair) to inside (fine linen, gold-covered wood).

Physical description: approximately 45 feet long and 15 feet wide (inner dimensions); oriented east-west, with the entrance to the east; surrounded by an outer court (approximately 150 × 75 feet, fenced with linen curtains on wooden posts); constructed by Bezalel and Oholiab and the skilled craftsmen of Israel, filled with the Spirit for the work (Exod 31:1–6).

Three zones of graduated holiness: (1) Outer Court — the bronze altar of burnt offering and the bronze laver (Exod 27:1–8; 30:17–21); where blood was shed and ceremonial washing occurred. (2) Holy Place — the lampstand (Exod 25:31–40), the table of showbread (Exod 25:23–30), and the altar of incense (Exod 30:1–10); where priests served daily. (3) Most Holy Place (Holy of Holies) — the ark of the covenant with the mercy seat and cherubim (Exod 25:10–22); where the divine glory resided and where the high priest entered once a year on Yom Kippur.

John 1:14 — “the Word became flesh and eskenosen [literally, tabernacled / pitched His tent] among us”; the verb is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew shakan; John is saying that Jesus is the living tabernacle, the place where the divine glory has taken up residence among humanity.

Hebrews 8–10: the tabernacle was “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (8:5); Christ as the high priest “passed through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands” (9:11); His blood, unlike the bulls and goats, purifies the conscience and secures eternal redemption (9:12–14).

Key Scripture

Exod 25:8 — "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them."

Heb 8:5 — "Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount."

Heb 9:1 — "Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary."

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The primary recovery needed is the typological reading that sees every element of the tabernacle as pointing to Christ, against allegorical flights that use the tabernacle to teach psychological spirituality rather than Gospel Christology.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery principle is typological fidelity: the tabernacle is a Christ-centered structure, and its proper exposition is the exposition of Christ in all His offices and saving work. The misuse to guard against is the allegorical approach (associated with the Keswick holiness tradition and some evangelical devotional preaching) that reads the tabernacle's structure as a map of the believer's spiritual journey from the outer court (salvation) to the Holy Place (consecration) to the Holy of Holies (deeper spiritual experience). While the graduated approach to holiness has genuine spiritual application, the primary movement of the typology is Christological and ecclesiological, not a program for the individual's sanctification stages. The outer court leads to the altar; the altar is the cross; the veil is torn; the access to God is through Christ's blood, once for all, not through progressive spiritual stages.

A parallel corruption is the use of tabernacle imagery in some charismatic contexts to teach a “presence of God” spirituality disconnected from Christ's finished atonement: the worshiper enters the Holy of Holies in praise and worship, passing through the outer court and Holy Place in stages of prayer and adoration. This misreads the tabernacle by ignoring what Hebrews does with it: the veil's tearing at the crucifixion (Matt 27:51) is the end of the old access-restriction, not the beginning of a new protocol of graduated worship-stages. The access to God opened by Christ's death is total, immediate, and unconditional for all believers (Heb 10:19–22) — the old graduated structure has been abolished, not replicated in a worship service.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mishkan (dwelling place) and 'ohel mo'ed (tent of meeting); Latin tabernaculum; tripartite structure (outer court, Holy Place, Most Holy Place) as graduated approach to the holy God; fulfilled in Christ as the true tabernacle and in the church as His body, the new temple.

expand to see more

Hebrew mishkan — dwelling place, sanctuary; from shakan (to dwell, to settle, to tabernacle); the root is the basis for Shekinah (the visible divine glory); the tabernacle is where YHWH “shekinah-s” — where His visible glory takes up residence; John 1:14's eskenosen (tabernacled) deliberately echoes this vocabulary

Hebrew 'ohel mo'ed — tent of meeting; the place where God met with Moses face to face (Exod 33:11); the relational character of the name complements the spatial character of mishkan: the tabernacle is simultaneously the place of divine dwelling and the place of divine encounter

Sinai pattern (Exod 25:40; 26:30; Heb 8:5) — Moses was shown the heavenly pattern and commanded to build according to it; the earthly tabernacle is therefore a shadow and copy of the heavenly reality; Hebrews develops this into its full typological argument: the earthly priests serve a copy; Christ ministers in the original

The veil (parochet) — the thick curtain (Exod 26:31–33) that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, embroidered with cherubim; its tearing at Christ's death (Matt 27:51) is the single most dramatic typological fulfillment in the Passion narrative: the barrier between God and humanity has been removed by the high-priestly sacrifice of the Son

Incarnation as tabernacling (John 1:14) — the Apostle John's use of eskenosen (“pitched His tent” / “tabernacled”) signals that the Word made flesh is the fulfillment of the tabernacle: the divine glory that dwelt between the cherubim now dwells in the person of the incarnate Son; the grace and truth Moses asked to see (Exod 33:18) are what the disciples saw in Him

Usage

"Expository preaching through Exodus 25–40 should be explicitly typological throughout: every piece of furniture, every fabric, every metal points forward to Christ and backward to the pattern shown on the mountain. The danger of purely archaeological or devotional treatments (what did the tabernacle look like? what can it teach us about prayer?) is that they miss the central claim of Hebrews: this entire structure was designed to be superseded by the reality it foreshadowed. Preaching that reads the tabernacle without Christ is reading shadow without sunlight."

"The three zones of graduated holiness in the tabernacle structure provide a theological map of the problem of sin and the solution of atonement. The outer court with the bronze altar is where the sinner meets the cost of approaching God — blood must be shed. The Holy Place with its light, bread, and incense represents continuous priestly mediation. The Most Holy Place is the divine presence itself, inaccessible except through blood. Hebrews reads all of this as anticipating what Christ accomplished: He is simultaneously the sacrificial lamb, the mediating priest, and the one through whose blood the curtain is torn. One Gospel preached through three zones."

"John 1:14's use of tabernacle imagery for the Incarnation (“He tabernacled among us, and we beheld His glory”) is the New Testament's most evocative connection between Old and New Testaments. The disciples who “beheld His glory” are in the position of the Israelites who saw the glory-cloud descend on the tabernacle (Exod 40:34–38): the same divine glory, now visible not in a tent but in a person. This is the claim that licenses all the typological connections: Jesus is the tabernacle, and every element of that structure is a lesson about Him."
